- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review

3	/**
4	 * Defaults, declared once and referenced by both schemas below.
5	 *
6	 * `rainGuard` is ON because the protective behaviour already shipped inside
7	 * `weatherRules` — defaulting it off would silently change the generator for
8	 * every existing user. `tempUnit` is Celsius because every stored threshold,
9	 * and the text sent to the model, is Celsius; the unit is a display choice and
10	 * never reaches the rules.
11	 */
12	export const PREFERENCE_DEFAULTS = {
13	  rainGuard: true,
14	  tempUnit: "C",
15	} as const;
16	
17	/**
18	 * The STRICT schema — the write path.
19	 *
20	 * `PreferencesSchema.partial()` validates an incoming patch, and it must reject
21	 * a bad value rather than quietly repairing it: garbage accepted here is stored
22	 * forever and paid for on every later read.
23	 *
24	 * Only preferences something actually reads belong here. A stored flag that no
25	 * code consults is a switch that lies to the user.
26	 */
27	export const PreferencesSchema = z.object({
28	  rainGuard: z.boolean().default(PREFERENCE_DEFAULTS.rainGuard),
29	  tempUnit: z.enum(["C", "F"]).default(PREFERENCE_DEFAULTS.tempUnit),
30	});
31	
32	export type Preferences = z.infer<typeof PreferencesSchema>;
33	
34	/**
35	 * The LENIENT mirror — the read path.
36	 *
37	 * `.catch()` sits on each field rather than on the object, so one malformed
38	 * value falls back on its own instead of discarding every other preference
39	 * alongside it. Defaults come from the same constant as the strict schema, and
40	 * `preferences.test.ts` asserts the two schemas keep identical keys, so adding
41	 * a preference to one and forgetting the other fails the suite.
42	 */
43	const LenientSchema = z.object({
44	  rainGuard: PreferencesSchema.shape.rainGuard.catch(PREFERENCE_DEFAULTS.rainGuard),
45	  tempUnit: PreferencesSchema.shape.tempUnit.catch(PREFERENCE_DEFAULTS.tempUnit),
46	});
47	
48	/** Read the stored bag, repairing anything unreadable. */
49	export function readPreferences(raw: unknown): Preferences {
50	  const source = raw && typeof raw === "object" ? raw : {};
51	  return LenientSchema.parse(source);
52	}

-- profiles: one row per auth user (id = auth.users.id).
-- Supabase Auth is the identity source — no clerk_id.
create table public.profiles (
  id              uuid primary key references auth.users (id) on delete cascade,
  display_name    text,
  handle          text unique,
  -- style quiz (the prototype's 6 questions)
  archetype       text,            -- Old Money | Smart Casual | Preppy | Streetwear
  palette         text,            -- Neutrals | Earth | Navy | Mono
  fit             text,            -- Tailored | Relaxed | Oversized
  dress_codes     text[],          -- Loungewear | Casual | Smart casual | Business | Black tie
  occasions       text[],          -- Work | Everyday | Weekend | Evening
  nogos           text[],          -- logos | skinny | bright | shorts | ripped | double_denim | graphic | square_toe
  formality_min   int default 1,   -- derived from dress_codes (for the generator's band)
  formality_max   int default 5,
  location_lat    double precision,
  location_lon    double precision,
  locale          text default 'en',
  style_dna       jsonb,
  ootd_streak     int default 0,
  onboarded_at    timestamptz,
  created_at      timestamptz default now()
);

alter table public.profiles enable row level security;

-- A user can read and update only their own profile.
-- (select auth.uid()) is the perf-optimised form; TO authenticated + ownership
-- predicate avoids the BOLA/IDOR trap; update needs both USING and WITH CHECK.
create policy "profiles_select_own"
  on public.profiles for select
  to authenticated
  using ((select auth.uid()) = id);

create policy "profiles_update_own"
  on public.profiles for update
  to authenticated
  using ((select auth.uid()) = id)
  with check ((select auth.uid()) = id);

-- Auto-create the profile row on signup. SECURITY DEFINER so the trigger can
-- insert past RLS; schema-qualified names + empty search_path per Supabase guidance.
create function public.handle_new_user()
returns trigger
language plpgsql
security definer
set search_path = ''
as $$
begin
  insert into public.profiles (id, display_name)
  values (new.id, new.raw_user_meta_data ->> 'full_name');
  return new;
end;
$$;

create trigger on_auth_user_created
  after insert on auth.users
  for each row execute procedure public.handle_new_user();

content.text:
Based on my review of the changed files:

**`app/settings/actions.ts`** — Server action is well-formed:
- Authentication is verified via `supabase.auth.getUser()` before any DB access
- The `profiles` table has RLS enabled with `auth.uid() = id` policies for both SELECT and UPDATE
- The `.eq("id", user.id)` scope defends in depth even if RLS were misconfigured
- Zod's default `strip` mode on `PreferencesSchema.partial()` removes unknown keys, so mass-assignment (e.g. `{admin: true}`) is not possible
- Object spread `{...readPreferences(row?.preferences), ...data}` copies own enumerable properties only — no prototype pollution surface
- `revalidatePath` targets are static string literals
- CSRF is handled by Next.js server action framework

**`lib/generator/rules.ts`, `lib/generator/candidates.ts`** — Pure functions over in-memory data. No sinks (no I/O, subprocess, SQL, URLs, HTML, filesystem, logs). The `decorrelatedStride` change and `rainGuard` threading are correctness fixes with no security surface.

**Test files** — Test-only, not in scope.

Notes I considered but decided are not security findings:
- The SELECT→UPDATE on preferences is not atomic (lost-update race between concurrent tabs), but the merge is scoped to the authenticated user's own row, so this is a data-consistency concern, not a security one.
- Supabase error messages are re-thrown via `throw new Error(error.message)` — Supabase update-error strings do not carry other users' data, and this is standard Next.js server-action practice.
